3fff0d81d164.exp: The isolated danger mark carries two black spheres one above the other. The yellow X belongs to special marks, cones to cardinals and the red sphere to safe water marks.

c1bdb2a52be6.exp: Special marks are yellow and their topmark is a yellow X. A black X, an O or a white one are not used in the IALA system.

23f84b776d9d.exp: Special marks carry a yellow X as topmark, the same as their buoy colour and light. A red or green X does not exist in IALA buoyage.

3733fc7dfb3e.exp: Renewable energy installations away from the coast are marked with special marks: yellow with a yellow saltire.

7931c24d1578.exp: Areas reserved for recreation are marked with special marks, yellow, with a yellow saltire (X) as topmark.

214a500bc0ec.exp: Special marks, which are yellow, have a yellow saltire (X) as topmark. Black cones belong to cardinals and black spheres to the isolated danger.

49af35e55272.exp: The topmark of special marks is the yellow X-shaped saltire. They are yellow buoys that are not for navigating by but for marking areas or installations.

8ceb1502284c.exp: Black and yellow bands indicate a cardinal mark: it warns of a danger and indicates on which quadrant one can navigate. It does not mark the port or a channel.

649182233ef2.exp: The beacon with green and red bands (green with a red band) is a junction mark with the preferred channel to port. The red one with a green band indicates the preferred channel to starboard.

2fb6d323243c.exp: The red sphere topmark belongs to the safe water mark (red and white bands): navigable water around the beacon. It does not indicate danger nor is it a mooring mark.

1310cb4a6db5.exp: The red sphere topmark on a buoy with red and white bands is a safe water mark. There is safe water all around it.

9b3d51e67cb5.exp: A mark with vertical blue and yellow stripes corresponds to a new danger (a newly discovered wreck), which does not yet appear on charts or in notices to mariners.

eadbbfb78426.exp: The mark with vertical red and white stripes and a red sphere is a safe water mark (navigable water).

b6ab848b0370.exp: Horizontal black and red bands with two black spheres: isolated danger. It is placed over a small danger and can be passed on any side.

313b2785c9d3.exp: Two cones with the points downward are the South cardinal: it advises us to navigate to the south, and the obstacle is to the north.

06b968863f8f.exp: Inside a port in Region A, a red beacon marks the port side of the channel (when entering). Green ones are starboard.

5ce4658a1e55.exp: Two cones with the points downward are the South cardinal (navigable water to the south), so the danger is to the north. Points downward indicate that you must pass to the south.

06dd7ed504b2.exp: The white light with Morse A (dot dash) identifies the safe water mark (navigable water). Cardinals use quick flashes; no other mark uses Morse A.

1a7e11740e5c.exp: Morse A (dot dash) is the rhythm of safe water marks, with a white light, which indicate that they can be passed on any side.

b14d5782f684.exp: The green beacon with a cone is a starboard mark when entering. When leaving port it must be left to port, so we bear away to starboard to leave the mark on our left.

965e7a0ad2a5.exp: The preferred channel to port is marked with a green light and a composite rhythm of 2+1 flashes. The rhythm is the same as for starboard and only the colour changes.

68c402a227a0.exp: Under Rule 5 of the COLREGs, every vessel, even at anchor, must at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing appropriate to the circumstances.

7adc5a25b4c6.exp: Two long blasts with an interval of 2 seconds, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, is the signal of a power-driven vessel under way but stopped and making no way through the water. One long blast is for when making way.

1779ebd6757c.exp: In a crossing situation between power-driven vessels, the one that sees the other on its starboard side is the give-way vessel. In the drawing B is on A's starboard side, so A must keep out of B's way.

cabf4d3a17a8.exp: Between sailing vessels with the wind on opposite sides, the one that has the wind on the port side keeps out of the way of the one that has it on the starboard side. In the drawing B has the wind on the port side, so it must manoeuvre.

43f7b76a664f.exp: A dredger shows two black balls on the obstructed side and two diamonds on the clear side. We must pass on the side of the diamonds, which is on our starboard side, so we bear away to starboard.

bb4772287264.exp: Three black balls in a vertical line indicate a vessel aground (by day). At night it shows two red lights and the anchor lights.

ac6dc205167f.exp: The courses of A and B cross, without being head-on or an overtaking situation. It is a crossing situation and the vessel that sees the other on its starboard side gives way.

f8ec72a8e7ae.exp: The vessel not under command is one that, through exceptional circumstances, is unable to manoeuvre and therefore does not keep out of the way. The vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre is so because of her work, not because of a breakdown.

4a9a591de6e8.exp: Under the COLREGs, 'under way' means a vessel that is not at anchor, made fast to the shore or aground. All three conditions must be met.

defb7c533d5f.exp: If the bearing of another vessel changes appreciably, there is no risk of collision. There is a risk if the bearing remains constant while it approaches.

e371c43e16e1.exp: The black cylinder is the shape of a vessel constrained by her draught. The vessel not under command carries two balls and the vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre ball-diamond-ball.

ef283fe7c354.exp: A continuous sounding with any fog-signalling apparatus is a distress signal and a request for assistance (COLREGs Annex IV).

b15a2bb02fdc.exp: A power-driven vessel gives way to a sailing vessel (Rule 18). We will manoeuvre to avoid a collision, unless the sailing vessel is overtaking or is a fishing vessel.

4449b8459867.exp: Overtaking another vessel obliges us to keep out of the way, whether we are under sail or not (Rule 13). The white stern light is what reveals that we are overtaking.

3606279abe40.exp: A is coming from abaft B, within the sector of 135 degrees on each side, so A is overtaking B and must keep out of its way.

c4f70177cbbc.exp: Three short blasts (· · ·) mean engines going astern. Two short is altering course to port, one short to starboard.

390152476a7c.exp: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line are those of a vessel not under command (NUC): an exceptional circumstance prevents her from manoeuvring as the COLREGs require (Rule 3 f). It is not the vessel constrained by her draught (three red lights) or the vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (red-white-red), which is so because of the nature of her work. Mnemonic: two reds, 'not under command, not my concern'.

4b720a15a27a.exp: In a crossing situation between vessels, Rule 18 sets a hierarchy: a sailing vessel must keep out of the way of one engaged in fishing. Even though a sailing vessel has priority over a power-driven vessel, fishing has priority over sailing, so the sailing vessel manoeuvres.

81f64855f5f7.exp: Rule 8 requires any action to avoid a collision to be positive, made in ample time and with due regard to the observance of good seamanship. Small changes of a few degrees go unnoticed by the other vessel, which is why the distractors fail. Key idea: clear, large and in good time.

e2afb1ca98cd.exp: The towing light is yellow, 135 degrees, and is placed above the stern light, with the same characteristics as it. It is easily confused with the white stern light, but the tug is distinguished by its yellow colour. Remember: towing, yellow.

78562f6b31f2.exp: Two cones joined by their points (hourglass shape) is the shape of a vessel engaged in fishing. If it were two cones joined by their bases (diamond) it would be a tug with a tow of more than 200 m. The vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre carries ball, diamond and ball; the vessel constrained by her draught, a cylinder.

1206b81bd17c.exp: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m in length may show, instead of the two white lights of larger vessels, a single all-round white light in the most visible position (Rule 30). All-round red lights indicate other situations, such as not under command or constrained by draught. It is only omitted if the vessel is less than 7 m and is outside a narrow channel or anchorage area.

3f91ac7b03a4.exp: Under Rule 3, 'under way' means that the vessel is not at anchor, made fast to the shore or aground. It includes a vessel that is stopped and making no way, as long as she floats free. 'Making way' is something else: it means the vessel is moving through the water.

828387660928.exp: To overtake on the starboard side in a narrow channel (Rule 34 c), two long blasts followed by one short are sounded, only if the vessel to be overtaken must act to allow it. Mnemonic: two long and one short, starboard (one side); two long and two short, port (two sides, two shorts). The vessel to be overtaken replies with ▬ ● ▬ ● if in agreement.

fb6f07be3706.exp: A tug whose tow exceeds 200 m shows as its shape a black diamond, that is, two cones joined by their bases (Rule 24). Cones joined by their points are the fishing vessel. A cylinder is the vessel constrained by her draught, and the purse seiner shows its gear with a single cone point up.

f76a714d2e05.exp: The lights of a sailing vessel are the sidelights (green and red) and the white stern light, with no masthead light; sometimes they are grouped in a tricolour lantern. Seen from ahead, only red and green are visible. Fishing adds vertical all-round lights and towing adds superimposed masthead lights and a yellow one, which do not appear here.

a3f6ce1ae58a.exp: A black ball hoisted forward is the shape for a vessel at anchor (Rule 30). A vessel not under command carries two balls in a vertical line; a vessel aground, three balls in a vertical line; a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, ball-diamond-ball. Remember: one ball, one anchor down.

abf75ece5217.exp: Two long blasts followed by one short indicate the intention to overtake on the starboard side (Rule 34 c). If it were two long and two short, it would be on the port side. Mnemonic: one short, starboard; two short, port. It is used in narrow channels when the vessel being overtaken must cooperate.

8b83b87c787e.exp: White over red is a pilot vessel on duty, which also shows her sidelights and masthead light. It is a power-driven vessel under way. Meeting head on, it is a head-on situation (Rule 14): both must manoeuvre, bearing away to starboard to pass port to port.

2d4bf210cc25.exp: When two sailing vessels have the wind on opposite sides, the one that has the wind on the port side keeps out of the way of the one that has it on the starboard side (Rule 12 a i). It does not matter who is to windward. Mnemonic: wind on the port side, you give way.

dd3de71c23da.exp: With the wind on opposite sides, Rule 12 requires the vessel that has the wind on the port side, which is us, to keep out of the way. The windward or leeward position only counts when both have the wind on the same side. Easy rule: port gives way to starboard.

17f6943a6864.exp: Red over green all-round lights, with the sidelights, correspond to a sailing vessel under way. As we have the wind on the starboard side, we have priority (Rule 12): if the other has the wind on the port side it gives way, or if it is the windward one, also. We maintain course and speed, while keeping watch (Rule 17).

03e40aba4132.exp: The masthead light is white and shows over an arc of 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side. The sidelights each cover 112.5 degrees, the stern light 135 and all-round lights 360. Sum: 112.5 + 112.5 = 225.

d9c38f387bc9.exp: In the International Code of Signals, flag N followed by C means 'I am in distress and require immediate assistance'. It is a visual distress signal, which is why it is used with flags together with the SOS signal or orange smoke. Other flags, such as warning or gale flags, are made up of other letters.

7d09fc7fe450.exp: In a head-on situation, Rule 18 applies first: the power-driven vessel keeps out of the way of the sailing vessel. The rule of both bearing away to starboard only applies between two power-driven vessels (Rule 14). Hierarchy: power gives way to sail.

6f8948e4b580.exp: A black ball forward is the shape of a vessel at anchor (Rule 30). A vessel not under command carries two balls, a vessel aground of 12 m or more, three balls. The black ball forward is 'anchor down'. A vessel with a pilot on board has no special shape.

62a5187f38f4.exp: Under Rule 9 b, sailing vessels and vessels of less than 20 m must not impede the passage of vessels which can safely navigate only within a channel or narrow fairway. Here there is no absolute prohibition on overtaking them, as distractor d suggests, but an obligation not to impede.

ed0df4dfa096.exp: The stand-on vessel must be able to manoeuvre on its own when the other does not do so and the approach is excessive (Rule 17 a ii). If the vessel that is not giving way is on our port side, we must not bear away to port because we would cross its bow. That is why the right manoeuvre is to bear away to starboard.

50c501941fc5.exp: The vessel with priority in a crossing situation (Rule 17 a i) must maintain course and speed, so that the other can calculate its manoeuvre. Changing course or speed would make it unpredictable. Only if the other does not manoeuvre and there is imminent risk does Rule 17 b come into play.

7fe86ced938c.exp: One long, one short, one long and one short blast (▬ ● ▬ ●) is the signal of agreement by the vessel about to be overtaken in a narrow channel (Rule 34 c ii). It is the reply to the overtaking signals: it means 'I agree'. It is different from the five short blasts of doubt.

d3f16632ac31.exp: A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing (Rule 18 b), whichever side she is on. That is why the sailing vessel manoeuvres. The wind rule (Rule 12) only applies between two sailing vessels. Hierarchy: sail gives way to fishing.

cf4d9bd8a8db.exp: A black diamond, two cones joined by their bases, is the shape of the tug when the tow exceeds 200 m (Rule 24 a). The vessel constrained by her draught carries a black cylinder. Cones joined by their points are the fishing vessel.
cf4d9bd8a8db.duda: The shape in the drawing is a diamond (two cones joined by their bases), which is that of a tug with a tow of more than 200 m (option a); the vessel constrained by her draught carries a cylinder. As with question 8, key d appears to be wrong.

840b684848f8.exp: The vessel we were crossing with has already passed us and is moving away, so the risk of collision is over. No manoeuvre is needed: we continue on course, watching that the situation remains clear (Rule 8 d).

f3d3f4fce5fb.exp: The shape of two black balls in a vertical line corresponds to a vessel not under command (NUC), which cannot manoeuvre. A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command (Rule 18 a), even if it would otherwise have priority. The tug and the fishing vessel carry different shapes.

381632b15338.exp: Safe speed (Rule 6) depends, among other factors, on visibility, traffic density, manoeuvrability, wind and sea conditions, and draught in relation to the available depth. Length, freeboard or power alone are not listed as determining factors in the rule.

2da420d43b83.exp: Two vertical red lights indicate a vessel not under command. If a red sidelight is also seen, she is making way and is being seen from her port side. Without way she would only show the two reds. Three vertical reds are the vessel constrained by her draught.

8aed70b98204.exp: A vessel constrained by her draught may show three all-round red lights in a vertical line (Rule 28), in addition to the normal lights, and by day a black cylinder. The vessel not under command shows two reds, the vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre red-white-red. It is not a vessel aground, which shows two reds, plus the anchor lights.

55fb53f78b18.exp: In restricted visibility, one long and three short blasts (▬ ●●●) is sounded by the towed vessel, if manned, immediately after that of the tug (Rule 35 e). Mnemonic: the tug gives one long and two short, and the towed vessel one long and three short. They are the two consecutive signals.

fac59ef48696.exp: Three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion', under Rule 34 a. One short is 'I am altering my course to starboard' and two short 'I am altering my course to port'. Mnemonic: the number of short blasts is the number of the side... one, starboard; two, port; three, astern.

e9caaf8f4bf6.exp: Two long blasts followed by two short (▬ ▬ ● ●) indicate, in a narrow channel, the intention to overtake on the port side of the vessel being overtaken (Rule 34 c i). For starboard it would be two long and one short. Mnemonic: two short, port.

09f2d5974681.exp: Under Rule 10 c, a vessel crossing a traffic lane of a traffic separation scheme shall do so on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow, to reduce crossing time. The smallest angle is used to join the lane, not to cross it.

5f6cb7cbce63.exp: In a crossing situation between power-driven vessels, the one that has the other on its starboard side keeps out of the way (Rule 15). Here the other crosses on our starboard side, so it is for us to manoeuvre, and we do so by passing astern of it. The shape in the figure does not give it priority over us.

72449f2775e3.exp: If the crossing vessel is on our port side, it is the one that has to keep out of the way, because it sees us on its starboard side (Rule 15). We are the stand-on vessel and must maintain course and speed (Rule 17 a i). We should not speed up or bear away.

252133b582dd.exp: The vessel crossing on our starboard side has priority, and we must keep out of the way (Rule 15). The most suitable manoeuvre is to bear away to starboard, passing astern of it, or to reduce speed (Rules 16 and 8). Bearing away to port would take us across its bow, and speeding up is imprudent.

2cf76828ea96.exp: If we see the other vessel's red light, we are seeing her port side and therefore she is on our starboard side: we must keep out of the way (Rule 15), bearing away to starboard to pass astern of her. We must not cross her bow or speed up.

b7b730f0dc9a.exp: A black cone with the point downward indicates a vessel proceeding under sail and engine at the same time; she is considered a power-driven vessel (Rule 25 e). A sailing vessel has priority over a power-driven vessel (Rule 18), so the other one manoeuvres. We, with the wind on the starboard side, would also have priority.

9f8bf3bd8a51.exp: Under Rule 8 d, the effectiveness of the action must be carefully checked until the other vessel is finally past and clear, that is, until there is no longer a risk of collision. It is not enough to see a change in bearing or to finish the radio communication.

3ce2295ec91e.exp: Under Rule 5, every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing, as well as by all available means, whether visibility is restricted or not. Being at anchor in fog does not exempt a vessel from it, and radar does not replace the look-out by sight and hearing.

cf853f439e0e.exp: Between a sailing vessel and one that is fishing, Rule 18 requires the sailing vessel to keep out of the way of the fishing vessel, even if they are meeting head-on. The rule of both bearing away to starboard applies only to two power-driven vessels.

b3ca4b056d98.exp: Two power-driven vessels meeting head-on with risk of collision (Rule 14) must both manoeuvre, each bearing away to starboard, so that they pass port to port. Mnemonic: to starboard, each on its right-hand side, like on the road.

7e497be9b763.exp: When it cannot be determined on which side the other sailing vessel has the wind and we see her to windward, we must assume she has it on the port side and manoeuvre ourselves (Rule 12 a iii). When in doubt, give way. We must not wait for the other to do so nor maintain course.

67d705333315.exp: A ringing of the bell for about five seconds followed by four short blasts is the signal of a pilot vessel at anchor in restricted visibility (Rule 35 i). Other vessels at anchor give only the ringing of the bell. Pilot vessels may add their identity signal of four short blasts.

3496829559a3.exp: The COLREGs, in Rule 3 c, define length as the length overall of the vessel. Length between perpendiculars or waterline length does not matter. The same applies to breadth: it refers to the maximum.

d896169817f0.exp: Red over white all-round lights are those of a vessel engaged in fishing (not trawling; trawling shows green over white). A power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of one that is fishing (Rule 18 a). It is the hierarchy: power gives way to fishing, even if the crossing is on the port side.

6de33aafc0ac.exp: If the vessel with priority does not maintain her course, the other must manoeuvre when it becomes apparent that she is not taking appropriate action (Rule 17 a ii). If she is on our port side, we should not bear away to port, because we would cross her bow; and that is why the recommended manoeuvre is to bear away to starboard.

16f22732311c.exp: The single shape indicates a vessel that, for manoeuvring purposes, is power-driven (for example sail and engine at the same time). Between two power-driven vessels in a crossing situation, the one that has the other on its starboard side keeps out of the way (Rule 15). Here the other has us on her starboard side, so she must manoeuvre.

d7520b15d120.exp: The single shape indicates a power-driven vessel for COLREGs purposes. She crosses us on our port side, so she sees us on her starboard side and she is the one who must keep out of the way (Rule 15). We, as the stand-on vessel, maintain course and speed (Rule 17 a i).

d8d1aba90497.exp: When two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side and there is risk of collision, the one to windward keeps out of the way of the one to leeward (Rule 12 a ii). Here the other is to windward, so she manoeuvres. The geographical direction of the wind is irrelevant.

5bb5ee4c8523.exp: A tug with a tow is a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, so a sailing vessel must keep out of her way (Rule 18 a), even though a sailing vessel normally has priority. The length of the tow does not change this hierarchy.

6e138218fc2f.exp: Under Rule 3 k, vessels are deemed to be in sight of one another only when one can be observed visually from the other. Detecting them by radar is not sighting, nor is distance a criterion. This definition separates Rules 11 to 18 (in sight) from Rule 19 (restricted visibility).

b7b15e886a34.exp: Red, white and red all-round lights in a vertical line identify a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (Rule 27 b). Mnemonic: red-white-red, restricted. The vessel constrained by her draught shows three reds, the vessel not under command two reds, and the tug, superimposed masthead lights and a yellow one.

db40f8ee1a01.exp: A dredger with two black balls on one side and two diamonds on the other indicates the side with the obstruction (balls) and the safe side on which to pass (diamonds). We must pass on the side of the diamonds; according to the figure, this is the port side, so we bear away to port. Never on the side of the balls.

3a2b864d15a2.exp: In poor visibility one must proceed at a safe speed adapted to the circumstances (Rules 6 and 19 b), which is not a fixed fraction of cruising speed. It must allow us to stop within an appropriate distance. The engine is kept ready for immediate manoeuvre.

566a7d0bac7f.exp: The towing light is yellow, has an arc of 135 degrees and is placed directly above the stern light (Rule 23). The white 135-degree light is the stern light. The yellow colour is what distinguishes them.

27b08c17d108.exp: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m shows, as a minimum, one all-round white light in the most visible position (Rule 30 e). Those of less than 7 m only omit it if they are not anchored in or near a narrow channel. Red lights are not used for anchoring.

77c450b94458.exp: The vessel not under command (NUC) carries two black balls in a vertical line, in the most visible position (Rule 27 a). One ball is for a vessel at anchor and three balls for a vessel aground. Ball and cone is the shape for another case. Mnemonic: two balls, two 'withouts' (without command).

3ad6d9f7d9db.exp: In restricted visibility, a vessel engaged in fishing sounds, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, one long blast followed by two short (Rule 35 c). The same signal is given by the vessel not under command, the vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, the vessel constrained by her draught, the sailing vessel and the tug (the latter with the one long and two short).

1e708c8a7081.exp: Flag A of the International Code of Signals means 'I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed'. A rigid replica of it, like the one in the drawing, is displayed on vessels engaged in diving operations (Rule 27 e). It does not indicate anchoring, grounding or constraint by draught.

0ab75a152b79.exp: A vessel of less than 20 m, such as sailing vessels, must not impede the safe passage of power-driven vessels following a traffic lane (Rule 10 j). It is an obligation not to impede, not to overtake them on a particular side or to use the coastal zone.

9f3c7785c4ec.exp: Alterations of course must be large enough for the other vessel to see them clearly: we must avoid a succession of small alterations of course (Rule 8 b). Passing astern or bearing away to starboard are, on the other hand, recommended practices.

6be6cbad95ae.exp: On a fishing vessel with gear extending more than 150 m horizontally, the cone with its point upward indicates the side on which the gear extends (Rule 26 c ii). That tells us where not to pass. The towing shape is a diamond, and sail and engine together is shown by a cone point downward.

61d50946b8f8.exp: Rule 13 requires any vessel overtaking another to keep out of her way, whatever the type of vessel. So, even though a sailing vessel normally has priority over a power-driven vessel, here the power-driven vessel manoeuvres, as she is the one overtaking.

10e315bfad3c.exp: Under Rule 13, any vessel overtaking another must keep out of her way, whatever the type of vessel. Between two sailing boats the overtaking one manoeuvres, not the one overtaken nor the one with the wind on the port side. A vessel is overtaking when she approaches from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam.

f4d8b359f039.exp: The COLREGs, in Rule 3 d, define breadth as the maximum breadth of the vessel, just as length is the maximum. Breadth between frames or other naval architecture definitions are not used.

99050241c1e6.exp: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line are those of a vessel not under command (Rule 27 a). A vessel at anchor shows white lights and a vessel aground, in addition to two reds, the anchor lights. A buoy or a vessel without complete lights is not identified by two reds.

87195d8ef0d9.exp: Green over white all-round identifies a trawler, which also shows sidelights. A power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a fishing vessel (Rule 18 a), even if the crossing is on the port side and therefore it seems we have priority. The hierarchy of Rule 18 prevails.

f526721ddc5e.exp: A tug with a tow is a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, and a power-driven vessel must keep out of her way (Rule 18 b). That the tow exceeds 200 m (diamond shape) does not change the obligation; it only indicates its length. Even if she crosses us on the port side, the hierarchy of Rule 18 prevails.

0d700188d535.exp: Superimposed white masthead lights and a sidelight correspond to a power-driven vessel. As her green light is visible, she is on our port side and sees us on her starboard side: she must keep out of the way (Rule 15). If she were a trawler, the lights would be green over white. That is not the case.

9a3e7d456699.exp: A power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel (Rule 18 a), regardless of which side she has the wind on or the side on which she crosses us. The wind rule (Rule 12) only applies between sailing vessels. We manoeuvre to avoid the collision.

52f47dc11462.exp: When two sailing vessels have the wind on opposite sides, the one that has it on the port side keeps out of the way (Rule 12 a i), and that is us. The windward or leeward position does not matter in this case. Mnemonic: wind on the port side gives way to starboard.

8aeb4eeaf609.exp: With the wind on the same side, the windward vessel keeps out of the way of the leeward vessel (Rule 12 a ii). We are to windward, so we manoeuvre, even though we have the wind on the starboard side. The geographical direction of the wind does not count.

bb4e241015b6.exp: A vessel aground shows anchor lights plus two all-round reds in a vertical line and has no way on. A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of one aground, as of a vessel not under command or restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (Rule 18 a). It is not a head-on situation.

e1b1a7221773.exp: Two long blasts followed by two short (▬ ▬ ● ●) indicate the intention to overtake on the port side of the vessel being overtaken, in a narrow channel, if she gives way (Rule 34 c i). If it were on the starboard side, it would be two long and one short. Mnemonic: two short, port.

5ca87a361cbc.exp: The tug, seen from astern, shows the white stern light and the yellow towing light above it, plus the towing masthead lights, and no sidelights are visible. The vessel constrained by her draught is distinguished by three vertical reds.

bd16314e8ec6.exp: The vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre carries red, white and red lights in a vertical line, in addition to her normal lights (Rule 27 b). None of this resembles the lights of the vessel not under command (two reds), the vessel constrained by her draught (three reds) or the tug (two whites and a yellow).

d05ce4a38aa0.exp: Two black cones joined by their points are the shape of a vessel engaged in fishing (Rule 26). Cones joined by their bases would be a tug with a tow of more than 200 m. The vessel constrained by her draught carries a cylinder.

3c1971841e61.exp: Ball, diamond and ball indicate a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre; if she also carries an anchor ball forward, she is at anchor (Rules 27 b and 30). Without way she would have only the first shape; making way, she would be under way. The vessel constrained by her draught carries a cylinder.

f4af3edb627e.exp: A sailing vessel seen from her port side shows only the red sidelight and the white stern light, with no all-round lights. The fishing vessel would additionally carry two all-round lights in a vertical line, and the towed vessel, with no masthead light, has no yellow light.

620a05364caa.exp: A fishing vessel seen from astern shows only the white stern light, together with the two characteristic vertical all-round lights (red over white, or green over white when trawling). No sidelights, since her stern is seen. A sailing vessel seen from astern would show only the stern light.

4659e9abe2f2.exp: A continuous sounding with any fog-signalling apparatus is a signal of danger and need of assistance (Rule 37 and Annex IV). It does not indicate anchoring or grounding, which are signalled with bell or gong. It is a distress signal.

2c0cc630699c.exp: Slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering the arms, outstretched to each side, is one of the signals of distress and need of assistance in COLREGs Annex IV. It does not indicate a steering failure or reducing speed. One must go to her assistance, or notify rescue services.

594d665b55a8.exp: Under Rule 9 b, vessels of less than 20 m in length must not impede the passage of those that can safely navigate only within a channel or narrow fairway. There is no obligation to overtake them on a particular side. The same applies to sailing vessels.

413a100f61b7.exp: Rule 18 establishes that a sailing vessel under way must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre and a vessel engaged in fishing. A tug with a tow is restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, so she would also be included. But the clearest and most literal option is the fishing vessel (Rule 18 b).

b90edd3ab76e.exp: If the cone with its point upward indicates gear extending more than 150 m, it indicates the side on which the gear extends (Rule 26 c ii). That is, the side on which we must not pass. Option a reverses it and d is the opposite.

a7756242f0b0.exp: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, the one that has the other on her starboard side keeps out of the way. If B is the vessel that has A on her port side, B has priority and maintains course and speed (Rule 17 a i). A must keep out of the way and not cross her bow.

1431bf9a45bb.exp: The vessel with priority in a crossing situation, which has the other on her port side, maintains course and speed (Rule 17 a i), so that the other can manoeuvre. She must not alter course or reduce speed. The five short blasts are for when the other does not manoeuvre and there is doubt.

361185b3247d.exp: Under Rule 10 d, vessels joining a traffic lane from the side shall do so at as small an angle as practicable to the general direction of traffic flow. They join at the ends only when possible; crossing at right angles is for crossing the lane.

cac93dcb68d5.exp: Safe speed (Rule 6) is the speed that allows one to take proper and effective action to avoid a collision and to be stopped within a distance appropriate to the prevailing circumstances. It is not called precautionary, reaction or prevention speed. It depends on visibility, traffic, manoeuvrability, sea state and draught.

1310f9201a38.exp: The stern light is white, placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, and has an arc of 135 degrees, 67.5 on each side from right astern. Together with the sidelights and the masthead light, it completes the lighting of a vessel. It is not called a sternpost light or a stern masthead light.

0ac476f61b7b.exp: A vessel constrained by her draught may carry three all-round red lights in a vertical line (Rule 28), hence 'all red'. They do not have white or green lights mixed in. By day she carries a black cylinder.

bc09c2de3bcf.exp: The expression 'under way' (Rule 3 i) designates a vessel that is not at anchor, made fast to the shore or aground. A vessel that shows only sidelights and a stern light, without red lights of other states, is simply under way. A vessel not under command would have two all-round red lights in a vertical line.

3d3836bbffa1.exp: White over red are the lights of a pilot vessel on duty, which is considered power-driven; the visible sidelights indicate she is coming from ahead. It is therefore a head-on situation between two power-driven vessels: both bear away to starboard (Rule 14).

d6cd03e65261.exp: If the crossing vessel comes from our port side, she sees us on her starboard side and must keep out of the way (Rule 15). We, with priority, maintain course and speed (Rule 17 a i). We must keep watch in case the other does not manoeuvre. We must not increase speed or bear away to port.

2a65cc3d9da1.exp: The drawing shows two white masthead lights and a red light: a power-driven vessel seen from her port side. If we see her red light, she crosses us from our starboard to our port side, that is, we have her on our starboard bow. According to Rule 15 (crossing), the vessel that sees the other on her starboard side is the one that gives way and manoeuvres. Mnemonic: the red light we see is a 'stop' light for her, but the obligation to keep out of the way is ours.

780a31bf980d.exp: The two vertical red lights plus the red sidelight correspond to a vessel not under command making way, seen from her port side. Under Rule 18, a sailing vessel must keep out of the way of vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre and vessels fishing. That is why the rule that the sailing vessel has priority over the power-driven one does not apply here: the vessel not under command cannot manoeuvre and the sailing vessel must give way to her, even though the latter is sailing on the starboard side.

b6be074010ca.exp: Green over white all-round, plus the green sidelight, is a vessel engaged in trawling seen from her starboard side. Rule 18 requires the sailing vessel to keep out of the way of vessels that are fishing, vessels not under command and vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre. The other shows no restricted-in-ability-to-manoeuvre signal (red-white-red), so the cause is fishing, not something else.

cecee844cb6a.exp: Each sidelight (green to starboard, red to port) covers an arc of 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam. Together the two add up to 225 degrees, which is exactly what the masthead light covers. The (white) stern light completes the remaining 135 degrees: 112.5 + 112.5 + 135 = 360 degrees.

f242b2ce1d87.exp: When a vessel in sight does not understand the intentions or manoeuvre of another, or is in doubt whether she is taking sufficient action to avoid a collision, she must sound the doubt signal: at least five short and rapid blasts (Rule 34 d). It may be accompanied by flashes of white light. Short blasts alone (one, two or three) mean 'I am altering course to starboard', 'to port' or 'operating astern', not doubt.

73a118a1575c.exp: Three white lights in a vertical line indicate a tug with a tow of more than 200 m, and the red light is the port side. A vessel constrained by her draught carries three all-round red lights, not three white ones. For the side: red is port and green is starboard, so the tug is seen from her port side.

74130084e733.exp: Rule 5 says that every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing, as well as by all available means appropriate to the prevailing circumstances. That is, look-out by sight and hearing always, not only in fog or only by day. That is why it is also required of a vessel at anchor or in good visibility.

bbb7a320a0fc.exp: Two white masthead lights in a vertical line, together with the green and red sidelights, make up the lights of a tug with a tow of less than 200 m seen from ahead. Those towing more than 200 m carry three white lights, and the fishing vessel shows red over white or green over white. The pilot on duty shows white over red.

6fcdee4b272d.exp: Green over white all-round, with a white masthead light above, is the vessel engaged in trawling. Mnemonic: trawling = green over white ('green, dragging along'), while other fishermen carry red over white. If she were over 50 m she would also carry the aft masthead light, and seen from astern the sidelight would not be seen.

83d61c71c6cf.exp: Green over white, both all-round, is the proper signal of the trawler. Other fishing vessels (purse seine, longline, etc.) carry red over white. Mnemonic: trawling is green over white; the rest, red over white. A dredger with an obstruction carries reds and greens in a vertical line.

c3cc27485658.exp: The towing light is yellow, with the same characteristics as the stern light but yellow in colour: arc of visibility of 135 degrees, placed above the stern light. It is not white (those are masthead and stern lights) nor all-round. Mnemonic: towing = yellow, like the light on the crane that pulls.

09184d85fd57.exp: A power-driven vessel under way but stopped and making no way, in restricted visibility, sounds two consecutive long blasts separated by about 2 seconds, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes (Rule 35 b). If she were making way she would sound a single long one. One long and two short is the signal for sailing, not under command, tug, fishing and similar vessels.

604321091895.exp: Three short blasts mean 'my engines are going astern' (Rule 34 a). One short is 'I am altering course to starboard' and two short 'to port'. Mnemonic: the number of blasts indicates the direction: 1 starboard, 2 port, 3 astern. It does not mean going ahead nor does it indicate a change of course.

327c3451b8b1.exp: In a traffic separation scheme, Rule 10 establishes that sailing vessels and vessels of less than 20 m in length must not impede the safe passage of power-driven vessels following the traffic lane. There is no need to overtake them on a particular side, nor is there an obligation to use shallow waters; the inshore traffic zone is an option, not an obligation. The rule is 'do not impede'.

6c5cb4eeafa1.exp: Rule 9 (narrow channels) says that vessels of less than 20 m in length and sailing vessels must not impede the passage of vessels which can safely navigate only within the channel or fairway. It is an obligation not to hinder, not to pass on a particular side. Think of it this way: the small one gives way to the big one, which has no option of leaving the channel.

c6a1646ecac2.exp: The vessel with priority (the 'stand-on' vessel, Rule 17) must maintain her course and speed, so that the other can foresee her manoeuvre and keep out of the way. She may only manoeuvre on her own if the other does not do so and collision is imminent. Changing course or reducing speed would make her unpredictable.

27e1a97c8d28.exp: If the bearing of an approaching vessel does not change appreciably, the two will meet at the same point at the same moment: there is a risk of collision (Rule 7 d). Constant bearing with decreasing range is the classic sign. It does not imply that she will pass us on a particular side.

51f1963ff3a5.exp: When a power-driven vessel overtakes a sailing vessel, Rule 13 governs: any vessel overtaking another, whatever her type, must keep out of her way. Here the overtaking vessel is the one under power, and she must manoeuvre. The rule 'sail has priority' (Rule 18) does not apply because overtaking prevails over any other rule of manoeuvre.

d1a853faad51.exp: Between any two vessels, the overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken (Rule 13), even if they are two sailing boats. Wind rules such as windward or port tack do not count; they apply in crossing situations between sailing boats, not in overtaking. It is overtaking when the overtaking vessel comes from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam of the other.

8e4193ff8a10.exp: The upper white light shining forward, with an arc of 225 degrees, mounted on the mast, is the masthead light (forward). The stern light is at the stern with 135 degrees, and the towing light is yellow. Green over white below is trawling.

20ccbf9e019f.exp: The white light forward is the masthead light, which covers an arc of 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side. The 112.5-degree one is a sidelight and the 135-degree one is the stern light. Mnemonic: 112.5 + 112.5 = 225, the same as the masthead light.

54dfa1701d1c.exp: A vessel at anchor of more than 50 m shows two all-round white lights; the forward one is higher than the after one (Rule 30). Mnemonic: the bow is the one that 'goes up'. She is not identified by quick flashes.

97b93a0b2227.exp: A sailing vessel that is also under engine is, for COLREGs purposes, a power-driven vessel and must carry by day, forward in the most visible position, a black cone with the point downward (Rule 25 e). Mnemonic: the cone downward 'points' at the engine, like a funnel feeding it. Two cones opposed by their points is fishing; the black ball indicates anchoring.

400e85728741.exp: B has A on her port side (A comes from B's left), so A has B on her starboard side and it is A that keeps out of the way (Rule 15). B is the vessel that maintains her course and speed (Rule 17). Mnemonic: the one that sees the other on her starboard side gives way.

877cb4b50f4e.exp: Under Rule 3, a power-driven vessel is any vessel propelled by machinery. A sailing boat that is under sail and engine at the same time is considered power-driven and must give way as such; she must also display the cone-point-down shape. That is why she is neither 'mixed' nor 'alternative'.

c9e0c1c1d5be.exp: The stern light is white, placed as far aft as possible, with an arc of visibility of 135 degrees towards the rear (67.5 degrees on each side). The towing light is yellow with the same arc. The sidelight covers 112.5 degrees and is green or red.

c13a8d39a73c.exp: All COLREGs shapes (ball, cone, cylinder, double cone) are black, so that they stand out by day against the sky and the sea. Red or white is not used. The associated drawing provides no additional information.

3398347c6bd4.exp: The masthead light is white, with an arc of visibility of 225 degrees forward. The sidelights are green (starboard) and red (port), the towing light is yellow and the stern light is white.

a2cd126b6dfb.exp: One long and two short in restricted visibility is the signal of a sailing vessel, and also of a vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, constrained by her draught, fishing or towing. Of the options offered, only the sailing vessel fits. A power-driven vessel making way sounds one long, and without way, two long.

d061adef3455.exp: The shape is a cone with the point downward, that is, a sailing vessel also under power, which is a power-driven vessel. Between two power-driven vessels in a crossing situation, the one that sees the other on her starboard side gives way. The other comes from our port side, so we are the vessel that she has on her starboard side: she sees us on her starboard side and she manoeuvres (Rule 15).

abf423c3c672.exp: A vessel overtaking another must keep out of her way (Rule 13), whatever the type of both. The lights in the drawing (red, green and white) are those of a sailing boat, but even if it is the sailing vessel that is being overtaken, overtaking prevails over Rule 18. That is why we manoeuvre, as we are the ones overtaking.

3822c2675042.exp: With two white masthead lights and the red port light we see the other vessel crossing from our starboard to our port side: we have her on our starboard bow, so we are the give-way vessel. The most suitable manoeuvre is a clear bearing away to starboard, made in good time, to pass astern of her. Bearing away to port would put us in front of her bow.

0c865eaf5f61.exp: The other sailing boat shows a red and a green light (sidelights). If we have the wind on the starboard side, we are sailing with the wind on the starboard side, and between two sailing boats with the wind on different sides the one that has it on the port side keeps out of the way (Rule 12 a i). The other, having it on the port side, is the one who must manoeuvre. Mnemonic: the one who sees the wind coming from the port side gives way.

8fd276e04203.exp: With the mainsail eased out to starboard, the other sailing boat has the wind on the port side. We have it on the starboard side. When two sailing boats have the wind on different sides, the one that has it on the port side keeps out of the way of the one that has it on the starboard side (Rule 12). The boom always falls on the side opposite to the one the wind comes from.

eb1d8cb4cd47.exp: With the mainsail to port, the other has the wind on the starboard side, the same as us: both on the same tack. In that case the one to windward (closer to where the wind comes from) must keep out of the way of the one to leeward (Rule 12 a ii). The other comes from our starboard bow, that is, from the windward side, so she is to windward.

da4e0c61cf19.exp: Under Rule 6, every vessel shall at all times proceed at a safe speed adapted to the circumstances, so that she can manoeuvre and stop in time. Restricted visibility or heavy traffic require reducing it even further, but the obligation is not limited to those cases or to night time.

163079b236a4.exp: Rule 32 defines a short blast as one of about 1 second, and a long blast as one of 4 to 6 seconds. Memorise: short 1 s, long 4-6 s. 2 to 3 s corresponds to neither.

ae6c85b821b5.exp: Under Rule 32, a long blast lasts about 4 to 6 seconds; a short blast, about 1 second. Mnemonic: 'short = 1, long = 4 to 6'. Any duration of less than 4 s is short.

5f538b5affc2.exp: The towing light is yellow and has an arc of visibility of 135 degrees, the same as the stern light, placed above it. The 225-degree light is the masthead light and the 360-degree one is an all-round light. Option d is text unrelated to the question.

ebd83884f26a.exp: Two balls in a vertical line on one side and two diamonds (biconical shapes) on the other, with ball-diamond-ball in the centre, is the shape of a dredger with an obstruction. The balls indicate the obstructed side and the diamonds the clear side on which one can pass. Constrained by draught carries a cylinder; not under command, two balls; fishing, two cones joined by the point.

0b4a0b87f629.exp: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line indicate a vessel not under command, and the third red light is the port sidelight, which only appears if she is making way. Without way she would only show the two reds. A vessel constrained by her draught carries three reds in a vertical line, but here one is a sidelight.

a548976ae511.exp: Two white masthead lights, one green and one red sidelight, make up the lights of a tug seen from ahead, with a tow of less than 200 m. A vessel constrained by her draught carries three red lights in a vertical line. Here no yellow light is visible either, because it would be seen from astern.

3cf19c31b561.exp: The yellow towing light above the white stern light, seen from astern, identifies a tug seen from behind. The pilot vessel carries white over red, the fisherman red or green over white and the sailing vessel red and green sidelights. Mnemonic: yellow = towing.

f6bfcd972266.exp: Two black balls in a vertical line are the shape of a vessel not under command (Rule 27 a ii). Mnemonic: two balls, two reds, not under command, just like the two red lights at night. One ball indicates at anchor; if aground she carries three balls.

c10ad50d49ab.exp: Ball-diamond-ball in a vertical line is the shape of a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre. The additional diamond at the yardarm indicates a tow of more than 200 m. A tug with a long tow that is also restricted in her ability to manoeuvre carries the two shapes combined, and the correct reading is d.

7540e4e4003b.exp: Rule 5 requires every vessel to maintain a look-out by sight and hearing at all times, and this includes vessels at anchor, since other vessels may approach. There is no exception for being at anchor or for rain.

c37a1ce053e6.exp: One white masthead light above another white one, plus the green sidelight, is a tug with a tow of less than 200 m, seen from her starboard side. If the tow were more than 200 m she would carry three white lights. The fishing vessel carries red or green over white, and the pilot vessel white over red.

f473421efe09.exp: Rule 18 establishes a hierarchy between vessels: the power-driven vessel gives way to the sailing vessel and both give way to a fishing vessel that is fishing. Therefore the sailing vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel engaged in fishing, regardless of which side she crosses on or where she gets the wind from.

f270200a4c78.exp: If we hear the fog signal of another vessel forward of our beam and cannot rule out risk of collision, we must reduce speed to the minimum at which we can keep steerage way and, if necessary, stop (Rule 19 e). We are not asked to alter course to either side, as the position of the other is not known, and to go astern only if essential.

27dbf27b172f.exp: The towing light is yellow with an arc of 135 degrees, like the stern light. Mnemonic: yellow, like a rope that drags; 135 degrees, towards the stern. The white ones of 225 degrees and 135 degrees are the masthead light and the stern light, respectively.

f251541975e1.exp: A vessel towing, like sailing vessels, vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre, vessels constrained by their draught and fishing vessels, sounds in restricted visibility one long blast followed by two short at intervals of not more than 2 minutes (Rule 35 c). Mnemonic: long-short-short, 'the one that is working or cannot manoeuvre'. Two long is engine stopped.

5fe65f4351ea.exp: A continuous sounding with a fog apparatus is the signal of danger and need of assistance (COLREGs Annex IV). It does not mean anchoring (which is a blast followed by a bell) or aground. It is not for warning of future fog.

7dd1375bed37.exp: Rule 9 says that sailing vessels, and vessels of less than 20 m, must not impede the passage of vessels which can safely navigate only within a narrow channel. There is no obligation to pass on a particular side or through shallow water. Mnemonic: the small one does not hinder the big one.

7cef8e043992.exp: When approaching a bend or an area of a narrow channel where other vessels may be hidden, the vessel must navigate with particular alertness and caution and sound one long blast (Rule 34 e). A vessel hearing the signal on the other side of the bend must also reply with one long blast.

7621ebb67e5d.exp: Two long followed by one short (– – ·) in a narrow channel mean 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side' (Rule 34 c i). Two long and two short would be on the port side. Mnemonic: one short = starboard; two short = port, as in the manoeuvring signals.

f0e07ee37f0c.exp: A vessel at anchor of 100 m or more in length must also use the work lights or equivalent to illuminate her decks (Rule 30 b). That is why the answer is yes, regardless of traffic or the master's judgement.

715a0550fb89.exp: An all-round white light with the sidelights is the regulation set for a power-driven vessel of less than 12 m in length, which may replace the masthead and stern lights with a single all-round white light (Rule 23 c). Those of more than 50 m carry two masthead lights. The pilot vessel carries white over red and the fishing vessel red or green over white.

5232151eb3e4.exp: A power-driven vessel (A) and a sailing vessel (B) meet head-on. In a crossing or meeting between a power-driven vessel and a sailing vessel, the power-driven one keeps out of the way of the sailing one (Rule 18), as the sailing vessel is the one with priority. Here the wind changes nothing: the hierarchy between categories rules.

4e44bfa73c3b.exp: The sailing vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel engaged in fishing (Rule 18 b). The hierarchy is: not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, fishing, sailing, power. Each one keeps out of the way of those above it in the list. That is why the sailing vessel gives way to the fishing vessel.

2a63ead4d52c.exp: A has B on her starboard side (B comes from A's right), so A is the vessel that must keep out of B's way (Rule 15). Remember: two power-driven vessels crossing, the one that sees the other on her starboard side gives way. The five-blast signal is only used if there is doubt about the other's intentions.

29bfab3ef249.exp: Rule 1 establishes that the COLREGs apply to all vessels upon the high seas and in all waters connected therewith navigable by seagoing vessels. They are not limited to merchant ships or to a size, nor do they exclude vessels not under command.

00b4af30b747.exp: Rule 27 e provides that a vessel engaged in diving operations, when her size makes it impracticable to display the shapes of a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, shall display a rigid replica of the International Code flag 'A', not less than 1 metre in height, visible all round. It must be rigid, not cloth.

cbb96ca3f6ba.exp: Under Rule 8, any action to avoid a collision must be positive, made in ample time and with due regard to good seamanship. It is not limited to one side nor to small changes of speed, which would not be properly detected by the other vessel.

e2265a22ad9b.exp: The shapes regulated by the COLREGs (balls, cones, cylinders, diamonds or double cones) are always black. That is what makes them visible by day against the sky and the sea. Red or green ones would be lights, not shapes.

5db0d27f28e1.exp: The masthead light is white and covers 225 degrees forward. The sidelights are green and red, the towing light is yellow and the stern light is white at 135 degrees.

4ae11c956725.exp: The stern light is white and is placed at the stern, with a 135-degree arc. The yellow one is the towing light, with the same characteristics, and the green and red ones are the sidelights.

5862bd7e475a.exp: Under Rule 3, a power-driven vessel is any that moves by machinery, and this includes a sailing boat using sail and engine at the same time. The pilot vessel, the vessel engaged in underwater operations or the trawler are vessels with a special lighting regime, but they are not in themselves 'the power-driven vessel' of the definition. The key is the simultaneous use of the engine.

da6e7eeed3d3.exp: Rule 18 only gives the sailing vessel priority over vessels 'engaged in fishing' which restrict their manoeuvrability. Trolling is recreational and does not restrict manoeuvrability, so that boat remains an ordinary power-driven vessel. The power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of the sailing vessel.

96e380ce9402.exp: If two sailing boats have the wind on the same side, the one to windward (closer to where the wind comes from) must keep out of the way of the one to leeward (Rule 12 a ii). Mnemonic: the one that is 'above' the wind gives way. It does not depend on length or geographical side.

848c7df5bd90.exp: If the bearing of the vessel changes appreciably, the other is not on a collision course and therefore there is no risk, even if they approach each other. When approaching very close (a very large vessel or a tow) there may be risk even with a change, but that is the exception. Equal speed is not a condition.

182976d38863.exp: The shape is a cone with the point downward: a sailing boat that is also under engine, that is, a power-driven vessel. Between two power-driven vessels, the one that sees the other on her starboard side gives way. The other comes from our port side, so she sees us on her starboard side and it is for her to keep out of the way. Having sails hoisted gives her no priority.

15fd5ecb204e.exp: The two masthead lights and the red light indicate a power-driven vessel seen from her port side: she crosses from our starboard to our port side. We have her on our starboard bow, so we give way (Rule 15). It is not a head-on situation, which would be bow to bow, nor a fishing vessel.

4653c1ac877e.exp: If the other has the wind on the port side and we have it on the starboard side, the one that has it on the port side keeps out of the way (Rule 12 a i). Being to windward does not change the rule: that rule is only used when both have the wind on the same side. Mnemonic: wind on the port side, give way.

4e5348d9e67b.exp: With the wind on different sides, the one that has it on the port side must keep out of the way of the one that has it on the starboard side (Rule 12). The other has the wind on the port side, so she gives way, whether she is to windward or to leeward. The windward criterion is only used if both have the wind on the same side.

91d328de2f01.exp: With the mainsail to port, the other has the wind on the starboard side, and we have it on the port side. The one that has it on the port side must keep out of the way of the one that has it on the starboard side (Rule 12). The boom always goes on the side opposite the wind, and from that the other's side is deduced.

f5166116b305.exp: To indicate agreement with the proposed overtaking in a narrow channel, long-short-long-short (▬ ● ▬ ●) is sounded, Rule 34 c ii. The overtaking vessel's proposal is different: two long and one short if on the starboard side, two long and two short if on the port side. A single long blast is the warning signal at a bend.

5ab5025d8a6c.exp: If we want to overtake another vessel in a narrow channel on her starboard side, when she has to act to allow it, we sound two long blasts followed by one short (– – ·), Rule 34 c i. To overtake on the port side it is two long and two short. Mnemonic: the number of shorts, 1 starboard, 2 port.

b587d6024b06.exp: On a dredger with an obstruction, the two biconical shapes (diamonds) or two green lights indicate the side on which one can pass; the two balls or two red lights, the obstructed side, which must not be used. So one passes on the side of the diamonds. Mnemonic: ball = blocked; diamond = clear way.

afb5ec0a18b9.exp: Under Rule 32, a short blast is about 1 second; a long one, 4 to 6. Mnemonic: short is 'one second'.

dc49a54bb733.exp: A black cylinder is the shape of a vessel constrained by her draught, which must display it by day (Rule 28). It is only used by power-driven vessels under way and at night they carry three red lights in a vertical line. It does not indicate anchoring (one ball) or aground (three balls).
